targets.authors: Luo, J., O’Connor, J., Melton, S., & Kowal, K. C.
targets.title: A statistical analysis of the campus-based open access fund at Boston College.
targets.evidence_quote: Given the differences between when authors can request funding and how their APCs are paid, as well as the similarities in award criteria, an interesting opportunity arose to test Luo et al.’s (2022) proposals for fund efficiency, specifically the time efficiency of different stages in the workflow, using similar data from the U of I – OAPF.
targets.outcome_quote: When comparing regression analyses, three areas of difference were noted between our study and Luo et al.’s (2022) results. The first area of difference is seen in applicant rank. Luo et al. found that student applicants were more efficient than early, middle, or late career applicants, while our research found that faculty applicants may have experienced fewer days between approval and expenditure than graduate students, staff, or postdoctoral applicants, but that the overall category does not appear statistically significant. Next, data from our study appear to indicate that returning applicants experienced more days between approval and expenditure than new applicants, e.g. those who had not sought funding before, while Luo et al. found that return applicant status was not significant.
targets.outcome_reasoning: The conclusion affirms the accepted/published article hypothesis, but this is one comparison, not an overall verdict. Discussion explicitly contrasts applicant-rank and returning-applicant results with Luo et al.; comparisons therefore partly agree and partly differ.

reasoning: Independent University of Idaho application data are used to test the Boston College findings. Other cited papers provide background or methods, not targets.
